source.title: Post-Hoc Reversal: Are We Selecting Models Prematurely?
source.authors: Rishabh Ranjan; Saurabh Garg; Mrigank Raman; Carlos Guestrin; Zachary Chase Lipton

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test-error trends over epochs and model widths, but adds post-hoc transforms and uses its own datasets and experimental settings rather than explicitly reproducing the original experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports epoch-wise and model-width test-error curves and compares their shapes across noise levels and post-hoc transforms. Results cited from other work are not included. Checkpoint-selection tables comparing selected models are not separate curve results.
record.test_reason: The paper studies post-hoc reversal, not double descent itself. It does report its own base test-error curves over epochs (CIFAR-10-N label sets, FMoW, Yelp, Income, Reddit-12k) and over ResNet18 width (CIFAR-10-N Worst). It states where double descent appears or not and how noise changes it. Real human label noise and post-hoc transforms make this a new setting with results on V1, V2 and V6 (T3, not T2: the method does not aim at the double-descent question).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that TS, SWA and ensembling can reverse base performance trends (post-hoc reversal), especially on noisy data. These transforms flatten or prevent double descent and fix loss-error mismatch. They propose post-hoc selection, which beats naive selection (e.g. >1.5× MMLU gain on LLaMA-2-7B instruction tuning). They also note TS can induce double descent in loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures test error across training epochs and a ResNet-width sweep, but adds temperature scaling, SWA, and ensembling and emphasizes noisy real-world datasets and post-hoc selection.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve patterns change with noise level, post-hoc transform, learning-rate schedule, dataset, and epoch.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying SWA or ensembling to the same base models flattens or removes the double-descent peak in test error, both epoch-wise (CIFAR-10-N Worst, FMoW) and model-wise (width sweep), on Yelp too.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc weight averaging or ensembling of trained networks suppresses the double-descent peak, consistent with a variance or memorization-driven peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Test loss shows double descent pre-TS but not post-TS on CIFAR-10-N Worst. TS creates double descent in some cases where none existed, and the Reddit-12k post-hoc curve shows double descent where the base curve does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether a double-descent shape appears depends on the metric and on post-hoc calibration or averaging of the model.

record.problems: Several relevant curves are presented in figures without exact numerical values in the text. Some reported settings show single descent, U-shaped overfitting, or no double descent; the study does not test a training-sample-size sweep.
record.rows_left_out: Selection comparisons in Tables 1, 5–11 report selected-model outcomes rather than full test-error curves; they were not added as separate curve rows. Other plotted datasets and metrics were omitted where the text did not explicitly describe a test-error trend relevant to the versions tested.

untested.parts: Only a ResNet18 width sweep on CIFAR-10-N Worst. No other architectures, datasets or noise levels, and no check that the peak sits at the interpolation threshold.
No check that the peak coincides with fitting the training set; curves are reported in figures only, with no peak magnitudes.
No non-deep model classes or capacity curves past interpolation across model classes.
EMC is invoked as an explanation (§5) but never measured or used to predict peak locations.
No multiple or triple descent. No sweep of tuned regularization; the Limitations note on heavy regularization is an assertion, not a result.

missing.what: Epoch-wise test-loss curves showing double descent pre-TS but not post-TS (loss, not error)
Base curves for the other CIFAR-10-N label sets (Aggre, Rand2, Rand3) and CIFAR-100-N, said to be in App. E but not described
Model-wise loss curves (pre- and post-TS) in the width sweep

record.verdict_notes: Double descent is a side observation here; all relevant evidence is figure-only, with no peak magnitudes in the text. The reader's notes for R8–R10 conflated post-hoc reversal with double descent. R5's state was wrong: the caption explicitly reports double descent for the Worst base error curve. Rows on transformed models were moved to fits_no_version because they measure an intervention, not the base phenomenon. The authors' EMC account (§5) is argument only, so it is not a test of V5. Tables 1 and 5–11 are selection results and correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study sweeps ResNet widths on CIFAR-10-N Worst, not a broad set of architectures, datasets, or the original settings.
Results cover the datasets and training runs in the paper; they do not establish the shape for all deep networks or settings.
No sweep varies the number of training examples to measure whether more data raises test error near interpolation.
The study does not test capacity curves across model classes at or beyond an interpolation point.
Effective model complexity is proposed as an explanation, but the study does not measure whether one complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
The study examines noise and double-descent curves, but does not test multiple or triple peaks or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this turns the second descent into a U-shaped curve.

rows.operation_detail: Sweep convolutional filter width and measure test error
rows.note: The paper describes model-size double-descent mitigation by post-hoc transforms; the figure shows the base error curve, with its best width stated as approximately 10.
rows.check: Figure-only. Double descent in the base width curve is implied by 'mitigate double descent', not stated outright. Best base width is ~10, so the second descent does not beat the first minimum.

rows.subject: ResNet18

rows.check: Single descent on clean labels: absent for V2. For V6 this absence at 0% noise is what a noise-driven account predicts.
